target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and boost turnout
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably solve the work-time barrier because private employers are generally not required to give paid holiday time off, so many low-wage workers in retail, food service, healthcare support, and similar jobs would still have to work or lose pay/job security.

target: AG1’s assumption that changing the calendar alone is an effective turnout reform
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday does not, on its own, address the real barriers to voting.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday meaningfully improves access for low-income workers
objection: A holiday is a blunt and unreliable lever for low-income workers because essential and customer-facing jobs still run, meaning the people most constrained by work schedules may not actually get the time flexibility the holiday is supposed to provide.

target: AG1’s claim that pairing the holiday with other reforms makes the holiday valuable
objection: If the holiday only matters when combined with enforceable time-off rules, expanded early voting, and registration fixes, then the holiday is redundant and can distract from the more direct reforms that actually solve the problem.

target: AG1’s claim that federal uniformity is a benefit of a national holiday
objection: Uniformity on the calendar is not the same as uniform worker protection, because a national holiday would still leave employer obligations uneven and would not guarantee that hourly workers can actually take time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces overall time pressure and logistical friction
objection: The holiday may not reduce time pressure at all for many voters because it can concentrate demand into a single day, which can lengthen lines and waiting times at polling places instead of easing them.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday is an incremental step worth taking even if it is not sufficient alone
objection: Making Election Day a federal holiday could misallocate political and policy attention toward a blunt calendar change instead of the more direct and effective levers, such as state time-off-to-vote laws, expanded early voting or vote-by-mail, and streamlined voting administration.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday helps many people and is therefore worthwhile
objection: A policy that helps people with flexible jobs or workplaces that close, while leaving inflexible hourly workers with the same work constraints, can widen rather than reduce turnout inequalities.

target: AG1’s claim that election administrators can manage turnout better on a holiday
objection: Better poll staffing does not solve the core problem for low-income workers, because the binding constraint is not just polling-place capacity but whether workers can safely leave work or access paid and flexible time to vote.

target: AG1’s argument that the holiday is still worthwhile because it can be paired with other reforms
objection: Saying the holiday must be paired with enforceable employer time-off, expanded early voting, and administrative fixes effectively concedes that the holiday itself is not the meaningful solution, so targeted reforms would be a more efficient first choice.
